final.headline: Miami Is The Best Team In The ACC, And If Not Them, Then Who?
final.dek: A viewer called it a bad prediction that Miami is far and away the ACC's best team with everyone else playing for second. That's my opinion, so I'll take the other side.
final.bodyMarkdown:
This one came from Spencer. He said, "One of the bad predictions out there is that Miami is by far the best team in the ACC, and everyone else is playing for second."

Spencer, Miami is the best team by far in the ACC, and everyone's playing for second. That's my opinion. So I am one of the many here, and you seem like one of the very few.

[EMBED:00:02:06]

But I know maybe where you're going with that. You did me the favor of typing one sentence. If you'd typed two or three more, you probably would have said things like, "We're still waiting on Miami to win the ACC. They still haven't ever won the conference title game. They were an overwhelming favorite last year and they didn't get it done." Although Clemson was in the mix last year.

All that having been said — a 13-3 season, 6-2 in the league, No. 7 in both preseason polls — I still think they're an overwhelming favorite to do this this year. So my question, rhetorically, because you're not here to defend yourself, would be if not them, then who?

[PULLQUOTE]

There is a scenario here where Darian Mensah has something happen to him. If he were hurt, if he were unavailable, there is a massive drop off between QB1 and QB2 at Miami. If that were to happen, and I don't know that anyone has a model to predict injury, then everything's off the table.

But if Darian Mensah is healthy, if this team is largely as is on paper, and you're telling me they're flat out not it and it's SMU or Louisville or Clemson or someone else, that's a model I want to buy stock in, because I can't see it.

— JP

blocks.text: Ryan said that one of the worst takes out there is Notre Dame being the best team if they were in the SEC, they would not survive that schedule.

I was on Colin's show and he was asking me, do you think that Notre Dame will just be a product of their schedule or are they a legit national title contender? So the quickest way that I could summarize my feelings towards Notre Dame is I said if they played in the SEC this year, I'd pick them to win the SEC.

I want to know this. What is it about the SEC schedule that Notre Dame's personnel wouldn't be able to survive? They're really good along the lines of scrimmage. The program is bedrocked in the very principles that it takes to survive that kind of schedule.

So I ask, what magic formula is it? What magic talent acquisition mechanism is it that Georgia possesses or South Carolina possesses or whoever you think is going to compete in the SEC that Notre Dame doesn't have? Is it a top quarterback? All they have is the Heisman Trophy favorite at Notre Dame. I don't think there is anything magical. In fact, I think Notre Dame would measure up very very comparably with the best in the SEC.
Now, if you want to take shots at their schedule, take shots at their schedule. But, as we have discussed many times on this show, there's a difference between a team and the schedule the team plays.

The example I always use, which is radical, is if I took the Seattle Seahawks fresh off a Super Bowl and I had them play University of Louisiana Monroe's schedule, you would have no respect for their schedule, nor should you, but that'd still be the Seahawks.

Just like Notre Dame this year, could play one of the softest schedules in the country. But if they're the best team in the country, they're the best team in the country. If they're a fraud, which is what many of you suspect, and they cakewalk their way through an inferior schedule, but they're not really legit — well, that's why we have a playoff. God invented the playoff to expose frauds.
So, that'll happen. If you're right and I'm wrong, that'll happen in the playoff. I highly suspect that Notre Dame will be a factor throughout.

final.headline: If Notre Dame Played In The SEC This Year, I'd Pick Them To Win It
final.dek: Ryan called it one of the worst takes out there. I said it on Colin's show and I'll say it here: I want to know what exactly it is about the SEC schedule Notre Dame's personnel couldn't survive.
final.bodyMarkdown:
Ryan said one of the worst takes out there is Notre Dame being the best team — that if they were in the SEC, they would not survive that schedule.

I was on Colin's show and he asked me: do you think Notre Dame will be a product of their schedule, or are they a legit national title contender? The quickest way I could summarize my feelings toward Notre Dame — I said if they played in the SEC this year, I'd pick them to win the SEC.

[EMBED:00:02:38]

What is it about the SEC schedule that Notre Dame's personnel wouldn't be able to survive? They're really good along the lines of scrimmage. The program is bedrocked in the very principles it takes to survive that kind of schedule. This is a 10-2 team from a year ago sitting at No. 4 in the preseason AP poll and No. 5 with the coaches.

So what magic formula is it? What magic talent acquisition mechanism does Georgia possess, or South Carolina, or whoever you think is going to compete in the SEC, that Notre Dame doesn't have? Is it a top quarterback? All they have is the Heisman Trophy favorite.

I don't think there's anything magical. I think Notre Dame would measure up very comparably with the best in the SEC.

If you want to take shots at their schedule, take shots at their schedule. Miami, Michigan State, Boston College — and beyond that, nobody else currently sitting in the AP top 15 before the playoff. Fine. But as we've discussed many times on this show, there's a difference between a team and the schedule the team plays.

[PULLQUOTE]

The example I always use is radical: if I took the Seattle Seahawks fresh off a Super Bowl and had them play University of Louisiana Monroe's schedule, you'd have no respect for their schedule, nor should you. But that'd still be the Seahawks.

Just like Notre Dame this year. Could play one of the softest schedules in the country. But if they're the best team in the country, they're the best team in the country. If they're a fraud, which is what many of you suspect, and they cakewalk their way through an inferior schedule — well, that's why we have a playoff. God invented the playoff to expose frauds.

If you're right and I'm wrong, that'll happen in the playoff. I have them ninth in my preseason bracket, behind Texas and LSU, so I'm not out here calling them the favorite. But I highly suspect Notre Dame will be a factor throughout.

— JP

And then right at close of business, just about an hour or so ago, we get word from the SEC, we're doing the same thing. And then some because they expanded it to basketball and everything else. And this is Ross Dinger. If you're watching on YouTube, you can see this. Ross reported that SEC presidents granted Greg Sanki, quote, pay close attention, kids, quote, full and unlimited authority, which includes the ability to suspend a school from competition. In addition to that, league bylaw grants the commissioner powers to deem a player ineligible, suspend coaches, administrators, etc. In other words, we're also going to have a policy against that.

Now, this was about five or so hours after Lane Kiffin showed up on Pat McAfee's show earlier today. And keep in mind, this is chronologically a little out of order, but I'm doing it this way for a reason. At the point in time Lane went on the show, we had not gotten word from the SEC. All the SEC had done was say, "Hey, we don't like this. This shouldn't happen." But they hadn't come out with the actual stance and policy and whatnot. So, listen closely. This was Lane Kiffin earlier today talking about all the latest news surrounding them possibly taking guys who had been cut from NFL teams in training camp and playing for LSU this season.

Yeah, there's a lot of parts of it that I don't like within that. I don't think professionals should come back to college sports and college football particularly. But in this instance, this is not professionals that have gone played seasons or just, you know, randomly file an injunction in a state to become eligible. This is part of a specific class that was ruled wrong by the NCAA that was supposed to be five for five. So, I think you're going to get in a really interesting situation if now as a conference you start to say, "Well, we're not going to follow this court order that's been issued and we're going to say that these kids that the court says can go anywhere, we're going to say no, you can't." That's that's some issues there.

Okay. So, what Lane is saying there has a germ of validity to it. What he's really saying is first off, he's trying to draw a delineation between guys who have actually played in NFL regular season games versus people who have tried out for teams and been cut and whatnot. And the language that the SEC later released sort of cut through all that cuz it was, if you've even tried out for teams, if you've even rubbed against, if you've declared for anything, you're ineligible. Okay. So they took care of the gray area there.

But what Lane's saying, which again in theory has some validity to it, is that the NCAA passed this rule, this five for five rule. And that whole thing was meant to say, okay, from this point forward, instead of doing the whole red shirt thing and the injury thing and all that, you're just going to have five years to play and that's it. However, you 2022 kids, you don't get that. Or also another explanation is some guys declared for the draft not knowing that rule change was coming and the argument there is well that's not fair because had they known the rule change was coming maybe they wouldn't have declared for the draft.

Is there some germ of validity in there? Of course there is. It doesn't bear the weight of greater scrutiny. The weight of greater scrutiny is forget the details. Is someone's feelings hurt? Maybe so. Could you argue something's a little unfair? Maybe so. But I'll see you with that and I'll raise you that these dudes were playing in NFL preseason games. These guys were in NFL preseason camp. They're professional athletes. They're not coming back to play college football. And then that's kind of when most people dust their hands and they absolve themselves. They kind of wash their hands of it all.

But this is the second time in six months that we've had this inflection point in college football where a famously well documented divided society has totally united. Brendan Sorsby bet on games. 95 plus% of the public said, "Yeah, he should never play college ball again." And Texas Tech/Brendan Sorsby tried to fight it and there was that whole kerfuffle out in Texas and everybody rose up against it. And then just when I thought I couldn't see that again, I got not just Lane and LSU, but I've got LSU among other programs looking at what they think is a very legal loophole to add players to their roster. And 95% of the public hated that too. This was even further down the road of that because this even united the conferences. These people have disagreed on everything and all of a sudden they agree on this. So hey, golf clap golf clap because it's the proper stance to have.

I will say this, as I said the other day, a lot of folks after we did our show the other night were in my DMs saying, "You took it easy on Lane. You took it easy on LSU." I don't care about Lane and LSU was my whole point. I will never count on any competitor in an ultra competitive arena voluntarily abiding by some code that you want them to abide by. Their only code, the only barrier is rules. That's it. Those are the entire reasons rules exist because you can't count on people to just do it the way you want them to, especially if it means foregoing an edge they think they can get.

I don't count on the competitors to do that. If you were against steroid use in baseball, you should be for a rule against steroids in baseball, which there was. So then when guys did it, it was a violation of rules and then you get popped. That's how it's supposed to work. Similarly here, it's just that we've had our shoelaces tied in college athletics because every time you try and enforce a rule or write a new rule, some lawyer comes along and you find out it's illegal.

So, here's what's happening right now. Yes, the Big 10 and the SEC came out with these policies, and it sounds like the Big 12 will do it, the ACC will do it. And the natural followup is this is probably not done. All you'll see is players sue conferences. In all likelihood, that's what you're going to see. I would expect it as early as tomorrow to see players trying to challenge conferences because conferences are acting in blatant violation of court rulings.

Now, here's my question. Famously, I am not a lawyer. Although Pate State has a heck of a law school, but I'm not a lawyer. But here is where my head is at on this. The enforcement threat from the Big 10 and the SEC, as I read it, is not on players. The enforcement threat was towards the schools themselves.

That's kind of how this reads to me. Full and unlimited authority, not to tell players they can't play. That's not what was in those graphics today. It was no, this is to you, the institution. You better not do it or there'll be consequences. So, I don't doubt that there'll be lawsuits. I don't doubt we'll hear a lot more noise about that.

But the other question that I'm asking is I kind of understand when they fought so hard for Brendan Sorsby, like that's your quarterback. I mean, that's a potential game changer. That's a potential season, playoff altering situation that Texas Tech had on their hands. I don't want to be disrespectful. I'm just rhetorically asking, in light of all this, is any school, LSU or anyone else, are any of them going to look and say, you know, it's worth it, I think we're going to pursue this anyway, I think we're going to go take some guys that were cut from NFL rosters and we're going to bolster ours a little bit. Yep, this is worth the risk. I don't know. Time will tell.

final.dek: Both leagues went from statements to policies in a single Tuesday, with the SEC granting Greg Sankey "full and unlimited authority." My question now is whether any program still thinks defying it is worth the risk.
final.bodyMarkdown:
This transfer portal thing's been a disaster. But boy, what a Tuesday it has been.

This morning, if you're like me, you woke up and before you even said hello to your loved ones, you checked your phone and saw a notification — probably from Pete Nikkos or maybe from Ross Dinger — and it said the Big Ten is deciding they're not going to let pro athletes come back and play college football. And everyone was like, golf clap. Then in this tribalistic world of ours, people started taking shots at the SEC, because you guys just put out a strongly worded statement last night, which was a layer or two of pathetic 'cause it looked like a statement and nothing else.

[EMBED:00:00:00]

The Big Ten definitely won the PR game on this day. They come out and say, "We're going to put out more than a statement. We're going to put out a policy." And their policy — I'm going to paraphrase, the details aren't all that important — was if you take some of these cats who have been cut from the NFL and you play them, we're going to suspend you as a head coach for up to 50% of your season and fine your institution millions of dollars. And they had unanimous support. Every president, every AD in the Big Ten.

Then right at close of business, about an hour ago, we get word from the SEC: we're doing the same thing. And then some, because they expanded it to basketball and everything else. This is Ross Dinger. Ross reported that SEC presidents granted Greg Sankey — quote, pay close attention, kids — "full and unlimited authority," which includes the ability to suspend a school from competition. League bylaw also grants the commissioner powers to deem a player ineligible, suspend coaches, administrators, etc.

Now, this was about five hours after Lane Kiffin showed up on Pat McAfee's show. Keep in mind, this is chronologically a little out of order, but I'm doing it this way for a reason. At the point Lane went on the show, we had not gotten word from the SEC. All the SEC had done was say, hey, we don't like this, this shouldn't happen. They hadn't come out with the actual stance and policy.

What Lane is saying there has a germ of validity to it. First off, he's trying to draw a delineation between guys who have actually played in NFL regular season games versus people who have tried out for teams and been cut. The language the SEC later released cut through all that: if you've even tried out for teams, if you've even rubbed against it, if you've declared for anything, you're ineligible. So they took care of the gray area.

But what Lane's saying is that the NCAA passed this five-for-five rule. That whole thing was meant to say, from this point forward, instead of doing the whole redshirt thing and the injury thing, you're just going to have five years to play and that's it. However, you 2022 kids, you don't get that. Another explanation is some guys declared for the draft not knowing that rule change was coming, and the argument is that's not fair — because had they known, maybe they wouldn't have declared.

Is there some germ of validity in there? Of course there is. It doesn't bear the weight of greater scrutiny. Forget the details. Is someone's feelings hurt? Maybe so. Could you argue something's a little unfair? Maybe so. But I'll see you with that and I'll raise you that these dudes were playing in NFL preseason games. These guys were in NFL preseason camp. They're professional athletes. They're not coming back to play college football. That's when most people dust their hands and absolve themselves.

But this is the second time in six months that we've had an inflection point in college football where a famously divided society has totally united. Brendan Sorsby bet on games. 95-plus percent of the public said he should never play college ball again. Texas Tech and Brendan Sorsby tried to fight it and there was that whole kerfuffle out in Texas and everybody rose up against it. And then just when I thought I couldn't see that again, I've got not just Lane and LSU, but LSU among other programs looking at what they think is a very legal loophole to add players to their roster. And 95% of the public hated that too. This one was even further down the road, because it united the conferences. These people have disagreed on everything and all of a sudden they agree on this. So golf clap, because it's the proper stance to have.

I will say this. A lot of folks after we did our show the other night were in my DMs saying, "You took it easy on Lane. You took it easy on LSU." I don't care about Lane and LSU was my whole point.

[PULLQUOTE]

Their only code, the only barrier, is rules. That's the entire reason rules exist — because you can't count on people to do it the way you want them to, especially if it means foregoing an edge they think they can get.

I don't count on the competitors to do that. If you were against steroid use in baseball, you should be for a rule against steroids in baseball, which there was. So when guys did it, it was a violation of rules and you get popped. That's how it's supposed to work. The way it's not supposed to work is, let's see, multivitamins are technically legal, I just don't think players should take those, that's a little bit of a health advantage. No — if it's that bad of an advantage, make it illegal. Similarly here, we've had our shoelaces tied in college athletics, because every time you try and enforce a rule or write a new rule, some lawyer comes along and you find out it's illegal.

So here's what's happening right now. The Big Ten and the SEC came out with these policies, and it sounds like the Big 12 will do it, the ACC will do it. This is probably not done. All you'll see is players sue conferences. I would expect as early as tomorrow to see players trying to challenge conferences, because conferences are acting in blatant violation of court rulings.

Now, here's my question. Famously, I am not a lawyer. Pate State has a heck of a law school, but I'm not a lawyer. Here is where my head is at. The enforcement threat from the Big Ten and the SEC, as I read it, is not on players. The enforcement threat was toward the schools themselves.

So if Bradley goes and tries out for the Atlanta Falcons and gets cut and then wants to go play for Auburn, if I'm Greg Sankey, I'm not punishing Bradley. I'm threatening Alex Gooish in Auburn and I'm saying, you do whatever you want to, but if you play him I have got — and I want to use the quote again — "full and unlimited authority" granted in a 16-0 unanimous decision amongst university presidents to act any way that I see fit, and I can suspend you and I can hold your institution financially responsible. At that point, play him if you want to, but there will be consequences.

That's how this reads to me. Full and unlimited authority — not to tell players they can't play. That's not what was in those graphics today. It was, this is to you, the institution. You better not do it or there'll be consequences. So I don't doubt there'll be lawsuits. I don't doubt we'll hear a lot more noise about that.

But the other question I'm asking is, I understand when they fought so hard for Brendan Sorsby. That's your quarterback. That's a potential season, playoff-altering situation that Texas Tech had on their hands. I don't want to be disrespectful. I'm just rhetorically asking: in light of all this, is any school — LSU or anyone else — going to look and say, it's worth it, I think we're going to pursue this anyway, I think we're going to go take some guys that were cut from NFL rosters and bolster ours a little bit. Yep, this is worth the risk.

For what it's worth, LSU and Auburn are scheduled to play October 24 at Auburn, noon Eastern. I don't know. Time will tell.

draft.headline: LSU Abstains as SEC Presidents Approve Penalties for Fielding Returning Pro Athletes
draft.dek: A day after joining a 16-0 vote to enforce the ban, LSU sat out the vote on sanctions that include a half-season coach suspension and a fine worth 50% of a sport's operating budget.
draft.bodyMarkdown:
SEC presidents voted Wednesday to attach real penalties to the conference's ban on fielding athletes who left pro leagues, and LSU abstained.

That matters because LSU is the school with the most immediate exposure. Lane Kiffin has recruited at least two players made NCAA-eligible by a Louisiana court injunction, and men's basketball coach Will Wade was pursuing another. The penalties now on the books: suspension of the head coach for half the season, a fine equal to 50% of that sport's fiscal-year operating budget, loss of conference voting privileges, and additional penalties as deemed appropriate. Commissioner Greg Sankey was authorized to enforce them.

The abstention is the tell. LSU was part of the unanimous 16-0 vote a day earlier to enforce rules against fielding athletes who dropped out of pro leagues. When the vote turned to what happens to schools that do it anyway, LSU stepped back.

The legal split is the whole fight. The injunctions, including the Louisiana one, are against the NCAA. The SEC and Big Ten have both interpreted those orders as not binding on individual conferences — meaning a player can be NCAA-eligible and still be unusable in the SEC. The Big Ten installed similar penalties when it voted earlier Tuesday. Lawyers for players argued the SEC's rule puts the NCAA in contempt, but as of Wednesday afternoon had not filed suit against the SEC. The Louisiana Attorney General's Office has not been involved.

Underneath all of it is the NCAA's June age-based eligibility rule, which gave athletes a five-year window but did not grandfather in Class of 2022 high school athletes who had already exhausted eligibility under the old standard. That gap is what sent players to court in the first place.

What's still unknown is most of the football. The players Kiffin recruited have not been identified, LSU has not said whether it intends to play them, and neither Kiffin, Wade nor the administration has commented publicly since Tuesday night's SEC announcement.

LSU went 7-6 in 2025 and opens 2026 against Clemson on Sept. 5. A half-season suspension, if it ever came to that, would cover a lot more than the opener.

SEC presidents voted Wednesday to approve penalties for schools that field athletes who dropped out of pro leagues. LSU abstained.

The vote has a direct LSU football connection: Lane Kiffin has recruited at least two players made NCAA eligible by a Louisiana court injunction. LSU men's basketball coach Will Wade was pursuing another such player.

The penalties include a coach suspension for half the season, a fine equal to 50% of that sport's fiscal-year operating budget, loss of conference voting privileges and additional penalties as deemed appropriate. Commissioner Greg Sankey was authorized to enforce the ban with penalties.

LSU had been part of a unanimous 16-0 vote a day earlier to enforce rules against fielding athletes who dropped out of pro leagues.

The injunctions, including the Louisiana injunction, are against the NCAA. The SEC and Big Ten have interpreted them not to cover individual conferences. The Big Ten adopted similar penalties when it voted earlier Tuesday to disallow former pro athletes from returning to rosters.

The NCAA passed an age-based eligibility rule in June that gave athletes a five-year window to play but did not grandfather in Class of 2022 high school athletes who exhausted eligibility under the previous standard.

The players Kiffin recruited have not been identified, and it is unknown whether LSU will field them despite the penalties. Neither Kiffin, Wade nor LSU's administration has publicly commented since Tuesday night's SEC announcement. Lawyers for players said the SEC's rule put the NCAA in contempt, but had not filed suit against the SEC as of Wednesday afternoon.

seo.title: LSU Abstains as SEC Approves Penalties for Fielding Returning Pro Athletes
seo.description: SEC presidents approved a half-season coach suspension and a fine equal to 50% of a sport's operating budget. LSU, which has recruited players covered by a Louisiana injunction, abstained.
